blocks.raw: <Tip>Memory aid: "Penny weight guides nail size (16d = 3.5 in common, 2.5 in finishing). A307 = 60k, A325 = 120k, A490 = 150k (bolt tensile grades). Wood-to-wood pull-out ≈ 25-50 lbf/in (nails) or 300-500 lbf/in (lags)."</Tip>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard mistake="Assuming all nail sizes sclea linearly with penny weight (e.g., 20d is 4 inches because 16d is 3.5 inches)." correction="Penny weight is non-linear and historically based on nail weight. Use ASTM F1667 reference tables; 20d common is 4 inches, but 10d is 3 inches, not 2.5 inches." />

props.mistake: Assuming all nail sizes sclea linearly with penny weight (e.g., 20d is 4 inches because 16d is 3.5 inches).
props.correction: Penny weight is non-linear and historically based on nail weight. Use ASTM F1667 reference tables; 20d common is 4 inches, but 10d is 3 inches, not 2.5 inches.

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard mistake="Specifying carbon steel fasteners for a typhoon-exposed building, assuming corrosion is only an aesthetic concern." correction="Corrosion reduces fastener cross-sectional area and pull-out strength, leading to structural failure during wind or seismic events. Use stainless steel or hot-dip galvanized fasteners in coastal environments." />

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard mistake="Using wood screws instead of lag screws to attach a heavy timber beam to a concrete foundation, assuming screw type has no structural impact." correction="Wood screws in concrete provide minimal pull-out strength and may strip out. Lag screws (or wedge anchors) are designed for timber-to-concrete and provide 300-500 lbf per inch of embedment." />

props.correction: Wood screws in concrete provide minimal pull-out strength and may strip out. Lag screws (or wedge anchors) are designed for timber-to-concrete and provide 300-500 lbf per inch of embedment.
